paragraphs: Graph clustering identifies groups of nodes that are closely connected. It supports applications such as community detection and collaborative filtering, but applying clustering algorithms to large graphs raises scalability problems. This paper proposes a divide and conquer framework intended to make existing graph clustering methods more scalable through distributed computation.

The contribution includes theoretical guarantees for recovering the clusters exactly. It also addresses the ability to find small clusters, rather than treating computational efficiency as the only objective. In the analyzed setting, the smallest recoverable cluster can grow more slowly than the square root of the number of nodes. The abstract contrasts this with standard methods that require clusters at least on that scale.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets support the framework’s efficiency and effectiveness. Together, the findings connect distributed graph analysis with both recovery guarantees and sensitivity to smaller groups. The small-cluster result matters because scaling a clustering method is more useful when it also preserves access to structure that standard approaches may miss.
icml-2015-a-divide-and-conquer-framework.tldr: A distributed divide and conquer framework scales graph clustering and provides exact-recovery guarantees that accommodate smaller clusters.

paragraphs: Principal component methods seek structure in data, but corrupted observations can interfere with that estimation. This paper develops a common framework for making several related methods robust to outliers. Its scope includes ordinary PCA, sparse PCA, and non-negative sparse PCA, so the contribution extends across methods with different structural requirements.

The contamination setting permits a constant fraction of observations to be arbitrarily corrupted. This is a strong form of contamination: the corrupted observations need not follow a convenient noise pattern. The theoretical analysis bounds estimation error using properties of the underlying data model, the particular PCA-like method selected, and the fraction of outliers. Robustness therefore comes with a quantified dependence on both the problem and the contamination level.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report strong performance for the algorithms produced by the framework. The main significance is the shared route to robustness: related PCA methods can be treated within one analysis, while their individual characteristics still enter the error guarantee.
icml-2015-a-unified-framework-for-outlie.tldr: A unified framework makes several PCA variants robust to a constant fraction of arbitrarily corrupted observations, with estimation-error guarantees.

paragraphs: This paper develops a common framework for sparse Gaussian process regression models that can provide useful predictions quickly and refine them as computation continues. This anytime behavior makes prediction quality a function of the time available, while keeping a chosen sparse model’s predictive distribution as the eventual target.

The authors reverse the usual variational construction: they start from the desired predictive distribution and build a concave objective whose maximum occurs there. They then derive stochastic natural gradient updates that improve the current distribution estimate. The framework guarantees asymptotic convergence to the predictive distribution of the selected sparse Gaussian process model.

A further efficiency result depends on specific decomposability conditions. When the chosen predictive distribution satisfies them, each stochastic gradient is unbiased and can be computed in time independent of dataset size. This is a per-iteration result, rather than a claim about total convergence time. Experiments on two real datasets containing millions of observations examine the resulting trade-off between prediction quality and computation time.
icml-2015-a-unifying-framework-of-anytim.tldr: An anytime framework incrementally approaches a chosen sparse Gaussian process predictor, with constant-time stochastic gradient computation under decomposability conditions.

paragraphs: The paper starts from a training difficulty: as earlier network layers change, the inputs received by later layers change too. The authors call this internal covariate shift and connect it to slow training, sensitivity to initialization, and difficulties with saturating nonlinearities. Their proposed response is to normalize inputs within the network.

Batch Normalization makes normalization part of the model architecture and performs it separately for each training mini-batch. The authors report that this permits much larger learning rates and reduces the care needed in initialization. They also find that it can remove the need for Dropout in some cases, making that benefit explicitly dependent on the setting.

On an image classification model, the method reaches the original accuracy with fourteen times fewer training steps and also improves final accuracy. An ensemble achieves 4.82% top-5 test error on ImageNet, exceeding the reported human-rater accuracy on that benchmark. These results demonstrate training and classification benefits in the evaluated systems, while the paper’s explanation centers on changing internal input distributions.
icml-2015-batch-normalization-accelerati.tldr: Batch Normalization normalizes layer inputs within mini-batches and substantially accelerates training in the reported image-classification experiments.

paragraphs: Advertising budget allocation asks how spending across media channels can influence as many customers as possible. A model with only one advertiser overlooks competition for those customers. This paper extends a bipartite influence model to include multiple advertisers whose allocation decisions interact, turning budget allocation into a game.

The resulting model is a potential game, which establishes the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium. Such an equilibrium represents a collection of choices where no advertiser benefits by changing its own choice alone. The authors also establish a price of anarchy of two: equilibrium social utility is at least half the optimal social utility within the model.

The framework can be simulated efficiently enough to analyze large markets. Simulations can estimate which channels an advertiser allocates resources to and which customers it influences. The contribution therefore combines a way to study competitive market behavior with guarantees about equilibrium existence and collective outcomes. Those guarantees concern the proposed game, giving its simulations a theoretical foundation.
icml-2015-budget-allocation-problem-with.tldr: A multi-advertiser budget-allocation game supports efficient simulation and guarantees equilibria with social utility within a factor of two of optimal.

paragraphs: The paper studies a thresholded version of matrix rank: count how many eigenvalues exceed a fixed positive value. The matrix is distributed indirectly, as a sum of matrices stored on separate machines. The central question is how much information those machines must exchange to estimate the count.

The authors establish a sharp separation between deterministic and randomized methods. Any deterministic algorithm for the studied problem requires communication proportional to the square of the matrix dimension, comparable in order to sending the entire matrix. Their randomized algorithm reduces the communication requirement to a quantity proportional to the dimension.

A matching lower bound shows that randomized methods also need at least linear communication in this setting. Thus the proposed communication scaling matches the best possible order established by the analysis. Numerical experiments demonstrate practical effectiveness as well. The result matters because it identifies randomness as a way to change the fundamental communication burden, rather than merely speeding up local calculations on each machine.
icml-2015-distributed-estimation-of-gene.tldr: Randomization reduces distributed generalized-rank estimation from quadratic to linear communication, matching a randomized lower bound.

paragraphs: Gaussian processes offer flexible spatial models, but their usual computation and storage costs make large datasets difficult. Kronecker methods exploit covariance structure to reduce those costs and support expressive kernel learning. This paper extends fast Kronecker inference beyond Gaussian likelihoods, expanding the kinds of observations that these scalable models can handle.

The approach combines a Laplace approximation with linear conjugate gradients for inference. Kernel learning uses a lower bound on the marginal likelihood. For observations on a dense grid with dimension D greater than one, the stated costs are O(D n^((D+1)/D)) operations and O(D n^(2/D)) storage. The grid structure is therefore a substantive condition behind the scaling result.

The authors also introduce a log Gaussian Cox process with expressive kernels for counts varying across space and time. Applied to 233,088 observations covering a decade of Chicago crime events, the model identifies seasonal patterns at multiple scales that vary by location. The reported forecasts are highly accurate for local areas over long ranges, illustrating the method’s spatial forecasting use.
icml-2015-fast-kronecker-inference-in-ga.tldr: Structured Kronecker computations extend scalable Gaussian process inference to non-Gaussian observations on dense multidimensional grids.

paragraphs: Frank-Wolfe solves smooth optimization problems using linear optimization steps instead of projections onto the feasible set. This is attractive when projections are expensive, but its general convergence rate can trail other first-order methods. The paper investigates whether the geometry of the feasible set can support faster convergence without replacing the basic algorithm.

For the strongly convex set setting analyzed, the authors prove a convergence rate proportional to one over the square of the iteration count. This improves on the general one-over-iteration rate, which is tight in the general case. The result connects faster progress to a particular geometric setting, so the general lower-rate result and the improved special-case result are compatible.

The paper identifies various balls defined by ℓp, Schatten, and group norms that have the required strong convexity and permit closed-form linear optimization. These examples connect the analysis to feasible sets where Frank-Wolfe’s computational advantage remains useful. The authors also show how their analysis yields several earlier fast-convergence results, providing a common explanation for them.
icml-2015-faster-rates-for-the-frank-wol.tldr: The paper proves a quadratic improvement in Frank-Wolfe’s convergence rate in its analyzed strongly convex set setting.

paragraphs: This paper studies how deep rectifier networks can transform pattern sets so that a linear boundary separates them while retaining control over distances. Its focus is the geometry of hidden representations: separating classes is useful, but the authors also want a guaranteed relationship between the transformed representation and the original data.

The analysis considers nonlinear hidden-layer transformations that approximately preserve distances. Under this construction, the margin of a linear separator at the output can be closely related to the margin of a nonlinear boundary in the input space. Consequently, maximizing the output classifier’s margin can approximately achieve maximum-margin classification in the original space.

The paper proves universal classification power for the distance-preserving rectifier networks it studies. It also uses distance preservation together with the output classifier’s maximum-margin property to justify generalization performance. The contribution is a theoretical connection between expressive hidden transformations and controlled classification geometry: the network can change which boundaries are linear while maintaining enough distance information to relate the two classification problems.
icml-2015-how-can-deep-rectifier-network.tldr: The paper connects distance-preserving rectifier representations with linear separability, universal classification power, and approximate maximum-margin classification.

paragraphs: The paper studies reinforcement learning with continuous states and undiscounted rewards. Its performance measure is regret, which tracks accumulated shortfall during learning. Guarantees in this setting depend on structural assumptions about rewards and state transitions, because a continuous state space requires learning behavior across more than a finite collection of states.

The proposed approach uses nonparametric kernel density estimation to estimate transition probability distributions. Its regret bounds depend on how smooth those distributions are. For one-dimensional states, earlier work under Lipschitz assumptions gave a bound of O(T^(3/4)) after T steps. Under smoothly differentiable transition probability functions, the paper obtains an asymptotic bound of O(T^(2/3)).

The smaller exponent means the stated regret guarantee grows more slowly with experience in that smoother setting. The improvement is therefore tied to assumptions that the transition estimator can exploit. The authors also derive improved bounds for higher-dimensional state spaces. Overall, the contribution links the regularity of transition distributions to stronger guarantees for learning in continuous environments.
icml-2015-improved-regret-bounds-for-und.tldr: Kernel estimates of transition distributions yield improved continuous-state reinforcement-learning regret bounds under smoothness assumptions.

paragraphs: High-dimensional data can contain a lower-dimensional nonlinear structure, described here as a manifold. The paper seeks a small collection of landmarks spread across that structure. Such landmarks are intended to capture its shape through a limited set of locations, making their placement central to the quality of the representation.

The method optimizes landmark positions in the continuous manifold space approximated from the data. It therefore permits locations beyond the observed data points. Each landmark moves according to the gradient of an objective inspired by active learning with Gaussian processes. The objective makes previously chosen landmarks repel a new one, encouraging it to explore other parts of the manifold.

The authors also derive a stochastic algorithm for large datasets. They demonstrate the approach on several collections, including the Million Song Dataset and New York Times articles. The key contribution is a continuous, objective-driven method for placing representative locations, with a selection mechanism that encourages coverage and an algorithm designed to handle substantial data volumes.
icml-2015-landmarking-manifolds-with-gau.tldr: Gaussian-process-inspired optimization places landmarks continuously along a data manifold, using repulsion to encourage broad coverage.

paragraphs: In a hidden Markov model, distinct hidden states can produce exactly the same output distribution. These aliased states complicate the question of what can be learned from observations. This paper focuses on models with exactly two aliased states and output distributions drawn from a parametric family, giving the analysis a precise scope.

For that class, the authors completely characterize minimality and identifiability. Minimality concerns whether a model needs its full hidden-state structure, while identifiability concerns whether observations distinguish its underlying parameters. These questions matter before designing a learning algorithm: they establish when the hidden description is essential and when recovering it is possible.

For a large family of parametric output distributions, the paper also provides efficient algorithms to detect aliasing and learn transition and emission parameters. The algorithms are statistically consistent, meaning their estimates approach the target parameters as data increase under the applicable conditions. Simulations illustrate the theory. The contribution combines structural characterization with constructive learning methods for a specific, difficult form of hidden-state ambiguity.
icml-2015-learning-parametric-output-hmm.tldr: For parametric-output HMMs with exactly two aliased states, the paper characterizes identifiability and develops efficient, consistent learning algorithms.

paragraphs: Mixed membership models describe grouped observations using mixtures of components. This paper introduces Markov M3, which learns relationships among those components through a fully connected graph. The model interprets assignment to components as a Markov random walk over the graph, allowing the assignment process to reflect connections among components.

The graph-based assignment differs from methods that organize components into a tree. The authors use a simple parametric model to represent complex dependencies while retaining full conjugacy. That property supports closed-form stochastic variational inference, connecting the model’s expressive dependency structure with a tractable procedure for learning from data.

Empirical results show that Markov M3 performs well against tree-structured topic models and learns meaningful topic dependencies. The significance is that relationships between topics become part of the learned model rather than being restricted to a tree organization. The reported results support the usefulness of this representation, while the inference construction explains how the added dependency structure can remain computationally manageable.
icml-2015-markov-mixed-membership-models.tldr: Markov M3 models mixed membership as a random walk over learned component relationships while retaining closed-form stochastic variational inference.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes TD(0) with linear function approximation, providing error guarantees after a finite number of updates. It gives both bounds on expected error and bounds that hold with high probability. This makes the analysis informative about learning progress before the limiting regime where convergence is usually considered.

The results expose a difficulty with step sizes proportional to the inverse iteration count. The analysis suggests this schedule cannot guarantee the optimal convergence rate without at least partial knowledge of the policy’s underlying Markov chain stationary distribution. The authors also analyze an iterate-averaged version of TD(0), which removes that step-size dependency while achieving the optimal rate.

A further contribution is a TD(0) variant incorporating a centering sequence. The authors establish exponential convergence in expectation for this variant, a different type of guarantee from a high-probability statement. Two synthetic experimental settings demonstrate the usefulness of the bounds. Together, the results connect finite-time analysis with concrete algorithmic changes intended to improve the convergence behavior of value estimation.
icml-2015-on-td-0-with-function-approxim.tldr: Finite-time TD(0) analysis motivates iterate averaging and a centered variant with exponential convergence in expectation.

paragraphs: The leading eigenvector problem usually concerns one matrix. This paper studies an online version in which matrices arrive in sequence and an algorithm predicts a unit vector for each one. Performance is compared with the leading eigenvector of the cumulative matrix, creating a benchmark based on the sequence as a whole.

Earlier regret-minimization methods face one of two difficulties: an expensive eigendecomposition at each iteration, or regret bounds with a large dependence on dimension. The proposed algorithms avoid expensive matrix decompositions while guaranteeing regret rates whose dependence on dimension is at most mild. This addresses both the cost of updating predictions and the quality of the cumulative performance guarantee.

The algorithms also admit implementations that exploit sparse data to reduce computation further. The authors extend their results beyond symmetric matrices to non-symmetric ones. The contribution is therefore a set of online methods that combine scalable computation with regret control, making the sequential eigenvector problem more suitable for large-scale applications.
icml-2015-online-learning-of-eigenvector.tldr: New online eigenvector algorithms avoid costly decompositions while maintaining regret guarantees with at most mild dimension dependence.

paragraphs: This paper combines pretrained visual features with online learning to track a target through video frames. Hidden-layer outputs from a convolutional neural network serve as feature descriptors. An online support vector machine uses those descriptors to learn an appearance model that distinguishes the target during tracking.

The method then converts the learned discriminative information into a target-specific saliency map. It back-projects CNN features with guidance from the support vector machine, connecting the feature representation to locations in the image. A generative appearance model constructed from this map produces the final tracking result in each frame.

The saliency map matters because it reveals the target’s spatial configuration, helping determine where the target lies rather than only whether its appearance is present. The authors report improved localization accuracy and the ability to segment the target at pixel level. Extensive experiments on a challenging benchmark show strong performance against contemporary tracking methods. The contribution links online discrimination, spatial saliency, and appearance modeling in one tracking procedure.
icml-2015-online-tracking-by-learning-di.tldr: An online tracker combines CNN features, an SVM, and target-specific saliency maps to improve localization and enable pixel-level segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an ordered stick-breaking process as a prior for Bayesian nonparametric models handling sequential mini-batches. Its atoms, the components carrying probability mass, appear in order and can be shared across batches. This sharing allows relevant statistical information to pass between batches as inference proceeds.

The weights are chosen so that the probability of adding new atoms decreases exponentially. Although the process is non-exchangeable, it admits predictive probability functions. The authors use these functions to build SUMO, a Gibbs-sampling MCMC algorithm that avoids imposing a fixed truncation on the component collection and applies broadly to Bayesian nonparametric models.

For Dirichlet process mixture models, SUMO improves perplexity over TSVI by 33% on three datasets with a million data points, using 3GB of RAM. The abstract describes these datasets as beyond the practical scope of particle filtering. The contribution combines a sequential prior with a sampling procedure, showing that this construction can support large-scale inference with the reported memory footprint.
icml-2015-ordered-stick-breaking-prior-f.tldr: An ordered stick-breaking prior enables SUMO, a truncation-free sequential MCMC algorithm demonstrated on million-point datasets.

paragraphs: The paper studies grouped observations that come with an ordered response, such as review text paired with a rating. Its goal is to learn statistical associations between the observations in each group and that group’s response. The proposed mixed membership models describe their joint distribution while explicitly treating the response as ordinal.

The ordinal treatment matters because the response categories have an order that the statistical model should handle appropriately. The authors contrast their approach with existing methods that rely on assumptions they identify as improper for ordinal variables. The framework is intended to support both prediction and diagnosis: estimating responses and extracting patterns associated with them.

The demonstration uses consumer reviews of mobile applications, combining unstructured text with ratings. The models recover recurring feedback patterns described as useful and meaningful. Comparisons with relevant existing methods show significant gains in predictive ability and knowledge extraction. These findings support modeling the relationship between grouped content and ordered responses in a way that respects the response type.
icml-2015-ordinal-mixed-membership-model.tldr: Ordinal mixed membership models jointly analyze grouped observations and ordered responses, improving prediction and feedback-pattern discovery in application reviews.

paragraphs: Recovering the lowest-rank matrix consistent with affine constraints is generally computationally hard. Replacing rank with the convex nuclear norm makes optimization more manageable, but recovery can fail for higher ranks or poorly structured constraints. Nonconvex alternatives can improve recovery while still encountering locally optimal solutions.

The authors derive a parameter-free algorithm resembling probabilistic PCA. Across a broad collection of empirical tests, it successfully recovers matrices even when the number of measurements equals the unknown matrix’s degrees of freedom. They report that this can happen despite highly ill-conditioned affine constraints, demonstrating success in settings that challenge the alternatives described.

The theoretical result is conditional: the authors identify circumstances where their cost function has a unique stationary point at the global optimum. They explicitly acknowledge that general recovery guarantees remain elusive for nonconvex methods. Applications to image rectification and a collaborative filtering benchmark provide additional demonstrations. The contribution therefore combines unusually strong empirical recovery with a structural explanation for favorable optimization behavior under specified conditions.
icml-2015-pushing-the-limits-of-affine-r.tldr: A parameter-free probabilistic PCA-like algorithm achieves low-rank recovery at the measurement limit in empirical tests, with conditional global-optimum results.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching reduces a large least-squares problem to a smaller one using random projections or sampling. Existing algorithmic results show that a small sketch can nearly preserve worst-case optimization error. This paper asks how that computational perspective relates to statistical accuracy when observations follow a linear model.

The authors develop a common framework for analyzing both perspectives. They examine prediction efficiency and residual efficiency, which assess different aspects of the sketched estimator’s statistical performance. They then derive upper bounds for several projection and sampling methods, allowing their behavior to be compared within the same framework.

The central distinction is that residual efficiency can be controlled with a sketch much smaller than the original dataset, while prediction efficiency typically requires substantially more samples. Thus preserving the least-squares objective closely does not automatically provide the same strength of statistical prediction guarantee. The abstract also notes that subsequent lower bounds establish the unimprovability of its prediction-efficiency upper bounds. The contribution clarifies which notion of accuracy a sketch-size guarantee actually supports.
icml-2015-statistical-and-algorithmic-pe.tldr: A unified analysis shows why small least-squares sketches can preserve residual quality while statistical prediction typically requires larger sketches.

paragraphs: The paper considers estimating leading principal components when high-dimensional samples arrive sequentially and memory is limited. The desired components are sparse, involving at most s nonzero attributes among p available dimensions. The task therefore combines structural estimation with the practical need to process data as a stream.

The authors develop two algorithms: streaming sparse PCA for data generated by a spike model, and streaming sparse ECA for an elliptical model. For k leading components, the stated memory requirement is O(pk), and the sample complexity is Θ(s log p). The algorithms are also designed for computational efficiency, making both storage and processing costs central to the contribution.

Finite-sample guarantees describe performance with a limited amount of data and imply statistical consistency in the high-dimensional regime under the analyzed models. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report good empirical performance. The result matters because it connects sparse component recovery with streaming constraints, showing how model-specific guarantees can accompany algorithms intended for memory-limited analysis.
icml-2015-streaming-sparse-principal-com.tldr: Two efficient streaming algorithms estimate sparse principal components with finite-sample guarantees under spike and elliptical data models.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how the shape of a variational inference objective affects the accuracy of learned marginal probabilities. It focuses on strongly convex free energies, whose curvature can be quantified by a convexity modulus. The authors connect this curvature to stability, giving a theoretical reason to design approximate inference objectives with stronger convexity.

Their high-probability bound on marginal estimation error is inversely proportional to the convexity modulus. This motivates objectives whose modulus remains constant as the graph grows. The paper identifies sufficient conditions for that property in tree-reweighted and counting-number entropy methods. These conditions establish ways to obtain strong convexity without claiming they are the only possible ways.

For counting-number methods, the analysis leads to an optimization framework that guarantees a specified modulus. Experiments report substantially more accurate marginal probabilities when learning uses free energies constructed through this framework. The contribution links an adjustable mathematical property of approximate inference to both an error guarantee and observed improvements in the probabilities produced by learning.
icml-2015-the-benefits-of-learning-with-.tldr: Strongly convex variational objectives yield stability-based marginal-error bounds and motivate a framework that improves marginal accuracy in experiments.

paragraphs: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo uses coherent Hamiltonian motion to explore a target distribution and construct Monte Carlo estimates. The abstract emphasizes that this can remain computationally efficient even for complicated, high-dimensional targets. Its usefulness therefore depends on how effectively the exploration produces estimates, alongside the computational cost of running it.

Large datasets can make the method too expensive, motivating approximations that use only subsets of the data. The paper examines this proposed shortcut and argues that naive data subsampling fundamentally compromises Hamiltonian Monte Carlo’s scalability. The issue is whether a cheaper approximation preserves the exploration behavior responsible for the original method’s efficiency.

The stated finding changes how the computational trade-off should be understood: reducing the data used by an approximation cannot by itself establish that the resulting sampler scales well. The paper’s contribution is an incompatibility argument concerning Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and naive subsampling. It directs attention to the relationship between approximation and coherent exploration when assessing whether a sampling method remains efficient for data-intensive problems.
icml-2015-the-fundamental-incompatibilit.tldr: The paper argues that naive data subsampling undermines the coherent exploration underlying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo’s scalability.

paragraphs: Many learning methods require solving an optimization problem whose solution changes with regularization or kernel hyperparameters. Selecting those parameters can require exploring a broad domain. This paper extends approximate solution tracking from a single parameter interval to domains with multiple parameter dimensions, while retaining guarantees on approximation quality.

The authors establish a lower bound on the complexity of approximate exploration. It is the product of the corresponding one-dimensional path complexities, capturing how the work compounds across parameter dimensions. They also prove a matching upper bound and turn it into an algorithm intended to be efficient both theoretically and practically.

The matching bounds show that the algorithm’s complexity meets the established limit in the analyzed setting. This makes the contribution more than a procedure for searching several parameters: it also explains the cost of that exploration relative to simpler paths. Experiments with kernelized support vector machines and the elastic net confirm the theoretical complexity analysis, connecting the guarantees to two parameterized learning problems.
icml-2015-tracking-approximate-solutions.tldr: Approximate solution tracking extends to multidimensional hyperparameter domains with matching lower and upper complexity bounds.

paragraphs: Yinyang K-means accelerates K-means clustering by avoiding distance calculations that are unnecessary for the final result. The method first groups the cluster centers. It then maintains lower and upper distance bounds between data points and centers, using those bounds to determine when further distance evaluation can be skipped.

The bounds are maintained efficiently, and the paper reports that this organization eliminates unnecessary calculations more effectively than earlier algorithms. Crucially, the method guarantees the same clustering results as standard K-means. Its acceleration therefore comes from reducing computation while preserving the clustering outcome, making it suitable as a replacement within an existing K-means workflow.

Across all tested datasets, cluster counts, and machine configurations, the authors report significant speed improvements over classic K-means and prior alternatives, describing an order-of-magnitude performance gain. The abstract also highlights simplicity and user control over overheads. These findings support the method’s practical appeal across the evaluated settings, with the result-preservation guarantee providing a separate reason that adopting the faster computation can be straightforward.
icml-2015-yinyang-k-means-a-drop-in-repl.tldr: Yinyang K-means skips unnecessary distance calculations while preserving standard K-means results and delivering consistent speedups across the tested settings.
